ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Streptococcus pyogenes is a Gram‑positive, beta‑hemolytic coccus that causes a spectrum of diseases from mild pharyngitis to severe invasive infections. Its virulence is driven by surface proteins, exotoxins and immune‑modulating factors.

sections.p: S. pyogenes is a cocci in chains, catalase‑negative, beta‑hemolytic on blood agar, and identified by Lancefield group A carbohydrate.
Key virulence factors include M protein, streptolysins, erythrogenic toxins, and hyaluronidase. These enable adhesion, immune evasion and tissue damage.
Spread by respiratory droplets or direct contact with skin lesions. Colonises throat or skin, then may invade deeper tissues.
From superficial infections (pharyngitis, impetigo) to invasive disease (necrotising fasciitis, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome).
Clinical features plus laboratory confirmation. In low‑resource settings, a rapid throat swab and clinical scoring guide treatment.
First‑line is penicillin or amoxicillin. For penicillin allergy, clindamycin or azithromycin. Supportive care for invasive disease.
Remember the 2–4 week lag between throat infection and rheumatic fever. Rapid tests guide therapy; culture remains gold standard.
b: ASO titre rises 2–3 weeks after infection

sections.p: Streptococcus aureus can cause erysipelas but is usually beta‑hemolytic and catalase‑positive.
b: Erysipelas – often GAS, not S. aureus

sections.p: ASO may remain high for months; a negative RADT does not exclude GAS if sampling is poor.
Treat the source, provide supportive care, monitor for complications. Avoid macrolides in severe disease due to toxin production risk.
Urgent care needed for signs of invasive disease: severe pain, swelling, rapid spread, fever >38.5°C, hypotension, altered mental status.
